Incendiary

/in-SEN-dee-air-ee/ - the stress falls on SEN · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Incendiary means deliberately designed to stir up anger or violence.

Stewards tore the incendiary poster off the canteen wall before the night shift arrived, but by then a hundred phones had photographed it.

Worked Example

Shakespeare stages it in the forum: Antony swears he has not come to stir anyone, then shows the crowd Caesar's torn cloak, reads them Caesar's will, and pauses in all the right places. He never says burn anything. By nightfall half of Rome is alight, which was the speech's whole design — each denial another armful of kindling, stacked where grief was already smoldering.

Incendiary is the exact word for that oration, because incendiary means deliberately designed to stir up anger or violence — the design is the point. Inflammatory language heats a room and may do it carelessly; incendiary language is aimed. Antony's speech was not a spark that happened to land badly. It was arson performed with sentences.

How Incendiary Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

inflammatory

inflammatory: heats tempers, sometimes carelessly; incendiary language is aimed at the explosion

rabble-rousing

rabble-rousing: works a crowd's anger out loud; incendiary can do it from a printed page

Antonyms

soothing

soothing: cools the room back down

placating

placating: gives the anger something so it will lie down

How Strong Is It? — pointed → provocative → incendiary

pointed vs. incendiary

pointed vs. incendiary: A pointed remark has an edge, but it means to score a point, not to start a fire.

provocative vs. incendiary

provocative vs. incendiary: Provocative goes further than pointed — it is built to get a rise out of people; incendiary claims the most: language meant to end in broken glass, or worse.

Sort It Out

Now place each word on the right side of incendiary.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — in-

Prefix — in-: in, upon

Root — cend

Root — cend: to kindle, to set glowing (Latin candere)

Suffix — -iary

Suffix — -iary: given to, having the character of

Put it together

Put it together: In- (upon) + cend (to kindle) + -iary (given to) = given to setting things alight. Latin incendium was a blaze, and English first used incendiary for literal fire-setters — the bomb sense survives. Applied to words, the metaphor keeps every part: the sentence is the torch, the crowd is the kindling.

Use the root in a new word: candle

Use the root in a new word: candle: A candle is the same root at its calmest — Latin candere, to glow, gives candela, the little glowing light.

Root Check

Word Choice

formal / journalistic, always an accusation

Incendiary is the strongest thing you can call language short of a criminal charge, and it accuses the author of design. Inflammatory may be an accident of tone; incendiary never is. The verb behind the effect is this unit's incite — incendiary words are the tool, inciting is the act — and a single act built to draw rage is a provocation.
